name: Artificial neuron (weighted sum plus bias, then an activation)
meaning: Each input x_i is multiplied by its weight w_i, the products are added, the bias b is added, and the sum z goes through an activation function f. With f = identity it is linear regression and with f = sigmoid it is logistic regression (both owned by classical-ml as models); here it is the unit every network is built from.
used_for: The building block of every neural network, from the 1943 McCulloch-Pitts unit to each hidden unit in a frontier LLM's feed-forward blocks. In the book: Chapter 12 (The artificial neuron; Should I go to the beach?); Appendix B (Weighted sum).

name: Dense (fully connected) layer, MLP composition and parameter count
formula: h = f(W × x + b), W of shape m × n ; batched: H = f(X × Wᵀ + b) ; MLP: y = f_L(... f_2(f_1(x))) ; parameters = m × n + m
meaning: A layer of m neurons reading n inputs is one matrix multiplication plus a bias vector, followed by an activation applied entry by entry. Stacking layers composes them into a multilayer perceptron (MLP); without the non-linear f, any stack collapses into a single linear map (Appendix B, Linear steps collapse).
used_for: MLPs, classifier heads, every projection inside a Transformer; it is why AI hardware is built around matrix multiplication. In the book: Chapter 12 (Layers, width and depth; Counting parameters; The forward pass: a layer is one matrix multiplication); Appendix B (One layer; Parameters in a dense layer).

name: Step activation and the perceptron learning rule
formula: step(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0, else 0 ; perceptron update: w ← w + η × (y − ŷ) × x , b ← b + η × (y − ŷ)
meaning: Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron applies a hard threshold to the neuron's sum (a sign variant outputs −1 or +1). Its learning rule nudges the weights by the error (y − ŷ) times the input, scaled by the learning rate η; it converges only when the classes are linearly separable, so it cannot learn XOR. The step has zero slope almost everywhere, which is why gradient training needed smooth activations.
used_for: Historical origin of neural networks, still taught in AIMA and Goodfellow; the threshold-plus-surrogate-gradient idea survives in binarized networks and spiking networks. In the book: Chapter 12 (A little history: from logic units to the perceptron; What one neuron can and cannot do; activation gallery, Step).

name: Sigmoid (logistic) activation and its slope
formula: sigmoid(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + exp(−z)) ; slope = sigmoid(z) × (1 − sigmoid(z)), at most 0.25 (at z = 0)
meaning: Squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1, so it reads as a probability or a valve setting. Its flat tails give near-zero slopes, the root of the vanishing-gradient problem in deep sigmoid stacks.
used_for: Yes/no output layers, the gates of LSTMs and GRUs, the output gate in Qwen's gated attention, DeepSeek-V3's sigmoid router scores, and inside SiLU/SwiGLU. In the book: Chapter 12 (Activation functions; gallery); Chapter 13 (Vanishing and exploding gradients); Chapter 14 (Gate); Appendix B (Sigmoid; derivative table).

name: Tanh activation
formula: tanh(z) = (exp(z) − exp(−z)) ÷ (exp(z) + exp(−z)) = 2 × sigmoid(2 × z) − 1 ; slope = 1 − tanh(z)^2
meaning: An S-shaped squash like sigmoid but ranging from −1 to 1 and centered on zero, which keeps the next layer's inputs balanced. Its slope is at most 1 (at z = 0).
used_for: Plain RNN updates and the candidate memory and output of LSTMs; the tanh approximation of GELU; logit soft-capping (Gemma 2) and Dynamic Tanh (DyT) reuse it as a smooth bound. In the book: Chapter 12 (gallery); Chapter 14 (Recurrent neural networks; LSTM).

name: ReLU and its variants (leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU, squared ReLU)
formula: ReLU(z) = max(0, z), slope 0 for z < 0 and 1 for z > 0 ; LeakyReLU(z) = max(α × z, z), α ≈ 0.01 ; ELU(z) = z if z > 0, else α × (exp(z) − 1) ; ReLU²(z) = max(0, z)^2
meaning: ReLU passes positives unchanged and zeroes negatives: cheap, with no saturation for positive inputs. Units stuck at negative input stop learning (dead ReLU); leaky ReLU keeps a small slope α for negatives, PReLU learns α, ELU curves smoothly to −α. Squared ReLU (Primer, 2021) squares the positive part.
used_for: Default in CNNs from AlexNet (2012) through ResNet, and in the original Transformer's feed-forward block; leaky ReLU in GAN discriminators and GAT attention scores; squared ReLU in NVIDIA's Nemotron-4 and the NanoGPT speedrun. In the book: Chapter 12 (gallery; Leaky ReLU definition; worked backpropagation through ReLU gates); Chapter 14 (ReLU definition); Appendix B (ReLU).

name: GELU (Gaussian error linear unit)
formula: GELU(z) = z × Φ(z) = 0.5 × z × (1 + erf(z ÷ sqrt(2))) ; tanh approximation: 0.5 × z × (1 + tanh(sqrt(2 ÷ π) × (z + 0.044715 × z^3)))
meaning: Weights the input by Φ(z), the probability that a standard normal variable is below z, giving a smooth ReLU that dips slightly below zero (minimum about −0.17). erf is the Gaussian error function; the tanh form is the fast approximation used in GPT-2's code.
used_for: BERT, GPT-2 and GPT-3, ViT and many vision Transformers; its gated form GEGLU is used in Google's Gemma models. In the book: Chapter 12 (gallery: GELU definition and values).

name: SiLU / Swish activation (with hard-swish and Mish variants)
formula: SiLU(z) = z × sigmoid(z) ; Swish_β(z) = z × sigmoid(β × z) ; slope of SiLU = sigmoid(z) × (1 + z × (1 − sigmoid(z)))
meaning: The input times its own sigmoid: smooth, slightly negative for negative inputs (minimum about −0.28), close to ReLU for large positives. β = 1 gives SiLU; hard-swish z × ReLU6(z + 3) ÷ 6 (MobileNetV3) and Mish z × tanh(softplus(z)) (YOLOv4) are cheap or smoother relatives.
used_for: The gate inside SwiGLU in Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral and Kimi models; EfficientNet; the activation in Mamba blocks. In the book: Chapter 12 (gallery: SiLU definition); Chapter 15 (Step 6: SwiGLU worked unit, Swish(2) = 1.762).

name: Softplus (smooth ReLU that stays positive)
formula: softplus(z) = ln(1 + exp(z)) ; slope = sigmoid(z) ; sharpened form: (1 ÷ β) × ln(1 + exp(β × z))
meaning: A smooth version of ReLU whose output is always positive, so it is the standard way to turn an unconstrained number into a positive one (a step size, a rate, a standard deviation).
used_for: Mamba's input-dependent step size Δ = softplus(...), decay parameterizations in Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet layers, positive variance outputs in probabilistic heads; inside Mish. In the book: Only here.

name: Gated linear units (GLU, ReGLU, GEGLU, SwiGLU)
formula: GLU(x) = (x × W + b) ⊙ sigmoid(x × V + c) ; SwiGLU(x) = SiLU(x × W) ⊙ (x × V) ; GEGLU(x) = GELU(x × W) ⊙ (x × V) ; ReGLU(x) = ReLU(x × W) ⊙ (x × V)
meaning: The input is projected two ways; one branch passes through an activation and multiplies the other branch entry by entry (⊙), acting as a learned volume knob per hidden unit. Dauphin et al. (2017) introduced GLU; Shazeer (2020) tested the variants and found SwiGLU and GEGLU best for Transformers.
used_for: SwiGLU is the feed-forward non-linearity of Llama 1-4, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Kimi and gpt-oss; GEGLU in Gemma; also the activation inside each MoE expert. In the book: Chapter 12 (SiLU definition mentions SwiGLU); Chapter 15 (Step 6: SwiGLU definition and worked unit).

name: Softmax layer (stable form, log-softmax and Jacobian)
formula: p_i = exp(z_i) ÷ sum over j of exp(z_j) ; stable: p_i = exp(z_i − max(z)) ÷ sum over j of exp(z_j − max(z)) ; ln(p_i) = z_i − logsumexp(z), logsumexp(z) = max(z) + ln(sum over j of exp(z_j − max(z))) ; ∂p_i ÷ ∂z_j = p_i × (δ_ij − p_j)
meaning: Turns a vector of scores (logits) z into probabilities that are positive and add to 1. Subtracting the largest score first changes nothing mathematically but prevents overflow; δ_ij is 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise. Sampling-time temperature is owned by the llm category.
used_for: The output of every classifier and LLM, the attention weights in every Transformer, and MoE routers. In the book: Chapter 12 (Softmax: turning scores into probabilities); Chapter 15 (Step D: softmax; Step 9: From vectors back to words, subtract-the-largest example); Appendix B (Softmax; Shift makes no difference).

name: Mean squared error loss
formula: MSE = (1 ÷ n) × sum over i of (ŷ_i − y_i)^2 ; slope for ŷ_i = 2 × (ŷ_i − y_i) ÷ n
meaning: Averages the squared gap between prediction ŷ_i and target y_i over n examples; squaring makes all errors positive and punishes big misses most. Minimizing it is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise; many texts use 0.5 × error^2 so the slope is just the error.
used_for: Regression heads, value-function training, the noise-prediction loss of diffusion models, feature and hidden-state distillation, autoencoders. In the book: Chapter 12 (Squared error, for predicting numbers; worked backpropagation uses 0.5 × error^2); Appendix B (Mean squared error; Squared-error slope).

name: Mean absolute error and Huber (smooth L1) loss
formula: MAE = (1 ÷ n) × sum over i of |ŷ_i − y_i| ; Huber_δ(a) = 0.5 × a^2 if |a| ≤ δ, else δ × (|a| − 0.5 × δ), with a = ŷ − y
meaning: MAE (L1 loss) grows linearly, so outliers pull less than with MSE. Huber is quadratic near zero and linear beyond the threshold δ, combining smooth gradients with robustness; smooth L1 is Huber with δ = 1 (some libraries divide by δ).
used_for: Bounding-box regression in Fast and Faster R-CNN (smooth L1), the clipped temporal-difference loss in DQN, robust regression and some image-restoration models (L1). In the book: Only here.

name: Cross-entropy loss for classification (negative log-likelihood)
formula: L = −sum over k of y_k × ln(p_k) ; one-hot target: L = −ln(p_correct) = −z_correct + logsumexp(z) ; batch loss = mean over examples
meaning: y_k is the target distribution (1 for the right class, 0 elsewhere unless smoothed) and p_k the softmax output. The loss is the surprise at the correct answer; computing it straight from the logits z with logsumexp avoids taking the log of a rounded-to-zero probability.
used_for: Image classifiers and every LLM's next-token pretraining and fine-tuning loss (the llm category covers its language-model form and perplexity). In the book: Chapter 12 (Cross-entropy, for choosing between options); Chapter 19 (Measuring surprise: the loss); Appendix B (Cross-entropy, one token and whole text).

name: Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with logits
formula: L = −[y × ln(p) + (1 − y) × ln(1 − p)], p = sigmoid(z) ; stable form from the logit: max(z, 0) − z × y + ln(1 + exp(−|z|))
meaning: The two-outcome case of cross-entropy, for a target y of 0 or 1 and predicted probability p. For multi-label problems it is applied to each label independently and summed; a positive-class weight handles imbalance.
used_for: Yes/no and multi-label classifiers, click-through prediction heads, discriminators, the per-pair sigmoid loss of SigLIP-style image-text models (the contrastive objective itself is owned by generative-classical). In the book: Only here (Chapter 12 covers cross-entropy in its multi-class form).

name: Label smoothing
formula: y_smooth_k = (1 − ε) × y_k + ε ÷ K
meaning: Mixes the one-hot target with a uniform distribution over K classes using smoothing ε (typically 0.1), so the model is never trained toward 100% certainty. With K = 10 and ε = 0.1 the right class gets 0.91 and each other class 0.01.
used_for: Inception-v3 (2016), the original Transformer (ε = 0.1), most modern image-classification recipes; rarely used in LLM pretraining. In the book: Chapter 13 (The regularization toolkit: label smoothing).

name: Focal loss
formula: FL = −α_t × (1 − p_t)^γ × ln(p_t), where p_t = p if y = 1, else 1 − p
meaning: Cross-entropy multiplied by (1 − p_t)^γ, which shrinks the loss on examples the model already gets right so training focuses on hard ones; α_t balances the classes. RetinaNet used γ = 2 and α = 0.25; γ = 0 recovers weighted cross-entropy.
used_for: Dense object detectors (RetinaNet, 2017, and many later detectors), class-imbalanced segmentation and medical imaging. In the book: Only here.

name: Margin-based metric-learning losses (contrastive pair loss and triplet loss)
formula: pair: L = y × d^2 + (1 − y) × max(0, m − d)^2, d = distance(f(x_1), f(x_2)) ; triplet: L = max(0, distance(f(a), f(p))^2 − distance(f(a), f(n))^2 + margin)
meaning: The pair loss (Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun, 2006; often written with a factor 0.5) pulls embeddings of similar pairs (y = 1) together and pushes dissimilar pairs at least m apart. The triplet loss asks an anchor a to be closer to a positive p than to a negative n by a margin (FaceNet used 0.2). InfoNCE and CLIP-style batch contrastive losses are owned by generative-classical.
used_for: Face recognition (FaceNet, 2015), Siamese verification networks, image retrieval, and sentence-embedding training (Sentence-BERT's triplet objective). In the book: Only here.

name: Backpropagation (the chain rule through layers)
formula: with z_l = W_l × a_(l−1) + b_l and a_l = f(z_l): δ_L = (∂L ÷ ∂a_L) ⊙ f'(z_L) ; δ_l = (W_(l+1)ᵀ × δ_(l+1)) ⊙ f'(z_l) ; ∂L ÷ ∂W_l = δ_l × a_(l−1)ᵀ ; ∂L ÷ ∂b_l = δ_l
meaning: The error signal δ (blame) starts at the loss and flows backward: each layer multiplies it by the transposed weights and by the activation's slope f', and each weight's gradient is its layer's δ times the input that flowed through it. This is reverse-mode automatic differentiation; one backward pass yields every gradient for about twice the cost of the forward pass.
used_for: Training every neural network; implemented by autograd in PyTorch and JAX. In the book: Chapter 12 (Backpropagation: passing the blame backward; The chain rule as gears; The worked example: one complete forward and backward pass; Checking backpropagation by nudging); Appendix B (Chain rule; Cost of a training step).

name: Gradients of a linear layer (matrix form)
formula: for Y = X × W + b (X: B × n, W: n × m): ∂L ÷ ∂W = Xᵀ × (∂L ÷ ∂Y) ; ∂L ÷ ∂b = sum over the B rows of (∂L ÷ ∂Y) ; ∂L ÷ ∂X = (∂L ÷ ∂Y) × Wᵀ
meaning: The batched version of the backpropagation step for one layer: the weight gradient and the gradient passed to the previous layer are each one matrix multiplication of the same size as the forward one. Two backward matmuls per forward matmul is where the 2N forward plus 4N backward (6N per token) rule comes from.
used_for: The backward pass of every dense layer, attention projection and expert; the basis of the 6 × N × D training-compute estimate (owned by compute-datacenter). In the book: Chapter 12 (worked example, Steps 3 and 6); Appendix B (Cost of a training step).

name: Gradient of softmax plus cross-entropy (p − y)
formula: ∂L ÷ ∂z_k = p_k − y_k ; likewise sigmoid plus binary cross-entropy: ∂L ÷ ∂z = p − y
meaning: When softmax and cross-entropy are combined, the messy Jacobian cancels and the error signal on each logit is simply predicted probability minus target. The same clean form holds for sigmoid with binary cross-entropy (and for squared error with a linear output, ŷ − y).
used_for: The first step of the backward pass in every classifier and LLM; fused cross-entropy kernels compute it directly from the logits to save memory on 100,000-plus-token vocabularies. In the book: Only here (Chapter 12's worked example shows the squared-error analogue, ŷ − y = −1).

name: Vanishing and exploding gradients, and backpropagation through time
formula: ∂L ÷ ∂h_1 = (∂L ÷ ∂h_L) × product over l = 2..L of (∂h_l ÷ ∂h_(l−1)) ; RNN: ∂h_t ÷ ∂h_(t−1) = diag(f'(z_t)) × W_hh ; BPTT: ∂L ÷ ∂W = sum over t of sum over k ≤ t of (∂L_t ÷ ∂h_t) × (product over i = k+1..t of ∂h_i ÷ ∂h_(i−1)) × (∂h_k ÷ ∂W) ; sigmoid bound: at most 0.25^L
meaning: The gradient reaching an early layer (or an early time step of an unrolled RNN) is a product of many per-step factors; if they are mostly below 1 it shrinks toward zero, if above 1 it explodes. Ten sigmoid layers can shrink it by 0.25^10 ≈ 0.00000095. Truncated BPTT stops the sum after a fixed number of steps.
used_for: Explains why deep sigmoid networks and plain RNNs were hard to train and motivates ReLU, careful initialization, normalization, residual connections, LSTM gating and gradient clipping. In the book: Chapter 13 (Vanishing and exploding gradients); Chapter 14 (Backpropagation through time, and why gradients vanish).

name: Xavier (Glorot) and LeCun initialization
formula: Xavier: Var(W) = 2 ÷ (n_in + n_out), uniform version W ~ U(−sqrt(6 ÷ (n_in + n_out)), +sqrt(6 ÷ (n_in + n_out))) ; LeCun: Var(W) = 1 ÷ n_in
meaning: Draws random starting weights whose spread shrinks with the number of inputs (fan-in n_in) and outputs (fan-out n_out), so activations and gradients keep roughly the same size layer after layer with tanh or sigmoid. Book example: 512 in, 512 out gives std sqrt(2 ÷ 1,024) ≈ 0.044. Orthogonal initialization is a common alternative for RNNs.
used_for: Keras's default (glorot_uniform); PyTorch's nn.Linear default draws from U(−1 ÷ sqrt(n_in), +1 ÷ sqrt(n_in)), a LeCun-style rule; many LLM configs instead use a fixed normal std such as 0.02 (initializer_range). In the book: Chapter 13 (Why the size of the random numbers matters; Xavier definition).

name: He (Kaiming) initialization
formula: Var(W) = 2 ÷ n_in, so std = sqrt(2 ÷ n_in) ; general: std = gain ÷ sqrt(fan), gain = sqrt(2) for ReLU, sqrt(2 ÷ (1 + α^2)) for leaky ReLU with slope α
meaning: Doubles the LeCun variance because ReLU zeroes about half of its inputs, keeping signal size steady through deep ReLU stacks (He et al., 2015). Book example: 512 inputs gives std 0.0625.
used_for: ResNets and most CNNs (torchvision's conv initialization), ReLU MLPs. In the book: Chapter 13 (Why the size of the random numbers matters; He definition).

name: Small initialization for residual branches (scaled init, zero init, LayerScale)
formula: GPT-2: residual output projections scaled by 1 ÷ sqrt(N_residual), in practice std = 0.02 ÷ sqrt(2 × n_layers) ; zero init: last norm gain γ = 0 in each ResNet block, ReZero y = x + α × F(x) with α = 0 at start ; LayerScale: y = x + diag(γ) × F(x), γ ≈ 10^-4 to 10^-6 ; DeepNet: y = Norm(α × x + F(x)), α = (2N)^(1/4)
meaning: Each residual branch adds into the same stream, so with N branches the stream's variance grows with depth unless each branch starts small. These rules start the network close to the identity map so a deep stack begins calm.
used_for: GPT-2, GPT-3, nanoGPT and Megatron-LM (scaled init), ResNet training at large batch (zero-gamma), CaiT, DINOv2 and other ViTs (LayerScale), very deep post-norm Transformers (DeepNet). In the book: Chapter 13 (Initialization: GPT-2 scaled the residual layers down by the number of layers).

name: Maximal update parametrization (μP) width-scaling rules
formula: with width multiplier m = width ÷ base_width: hidden-weight init variance ∝ 1 ÷ fan_in ; Adam learning rate of hidden matrices = η_base ÷ m ; output logits multiplied by 1 ÷ m ; attention scores scaled by 1 ÷ d_head instead of 1 ÷ sqrt(d_head)
meaning: Rescales initialization, per-layer learning rates and multipliers with model width so that every layer keeps learning at the same rate as the model grows; then the best hyperparameters found on a small proxy model transfer to the large one (μTransfer, Yang et al. 2022).
used_for: Hyperparameter transfer for large runs, publicly in Cerebras-GPT, MiniCPM and Microsoft research models. In the book: Chapter 19 (The settings: μP definition).

name: Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
formula: g = (1 ÷ B) × sum over i in the batch of ∇_θ ℓ(x_i, y_i; θ) ; θ ← θ − η × g
meaning: Estimate the gradient of the loss from a random mini-batch of B examples instead of the whole dataset, then step every parameter θ against it with learning rate η. B = N is full-batch gradient descent (foundations covers the general method); B = 1 is pure SGD; one pass over the data is an epoch.
used_for: The inner loop of all neural-network training; plain SGD still trains many small models, and every adaptive optimizer below modifies this step. In the book: Chapter 12 (Gradient descent: walking downhill in fog; The training loop: batches, steps and epochs); Chapter 13 (The trouble with plain SGD); Appendix B (Gradient descent step).

name: Momentum (heavy ball) and Nesterov momentum
formula: v ← μ × v + g ; θ ← θ − η × v (equivalently v ← μ × v − η × g, θ ← θ + v) ; Nesterov: gradient taken at the look-ahead point θ − η × μ × v, in PyTorch form θ ← θ − η × (g + μ × v_new)
meaning: Keeps a running velocity v that accumulates past gradients with decay μ (typically 0.9), so steps speed up along consistent directions and zig-zags cancel. Nesterov's version evaluates the slope where the momentum is about to carry you, which corrects overshoot earlier.
used_for: SGD with momentum trained the 2010s image networks (ResNet on ImageNet); momentum is built into Adam, Lion and Muon, and Muon uses the Nesterov form by default (μ = 0.95 in PyTorch). In the book: Chapter 13 (Momentum: a rolling ball; optimizer family tree).

name: AdaGrad
formula: G ← G + g^2 ; θ ← θ − η × g ÷ (sqrt(G) + ε)
meaning: Each parameter keeps the running sum G of its squared gradients (entry by entry) and divides its step by sqrt(G), so frequently updated parameters slow down and rare ones keep larger steps; ε avoids division by zero. Steps shrink forever, which RMSProp fixes.
used_for: Sparse features and embedding tables (GloVe was trained with AdaGrad; row-wise AdaGrad is common for large recommender embeddings). In the book: Chapter 13 (mentioned in the optimizer family).

name: RMSProp
formula: v ← ρ × v + (1 − ρ) × g^2 ; θ ← θ − η × g ÷ (sqrt(v) + ε)
meaning: Like AdaGrad but with an exponential moving average of squared gradients (decay ρ, 0.9 in Hinton's 2012 lecture, 0.99 by default in PyTorch), so the per-parameter step size adapts without shrinking to zero.
used_for: Early deep reinforcement learning (DQN) and RNN training; the direct ancestor of Adam's second moment. In the book: Chapter 13 (optimizer family tree, RMSProp 2012).

name: Adam (with bias correction)
meaning: Keeps a moving average m of gradients (momentum) and v of squared gradients (per-parameter scale), divides one by the square root of the other, and corrects both for starting at zero (at step t = 1, m̂ equals g exactly). Defaults β_1 = 0.9, β_2 = 0.999, ε = 10^-8; LLM runs usually use β_2 = 0.95. Variants: AMSGrad, Adamax, NAdam.
used_for: The default deep-learning optimizer from 2014 for about a decade; its two state numbers per parameter drive the 16-bytes-per-parameter training-memory rule. In the book: Chapter 13 (Adam: a separate stride for every knob); Appendix B (Training memory).

name: AdamW (Adam with decoupled weight decay)
formula: θ ← θ − η × (m̂ ÷ (sqrt(v̂) + ε) + λ × θ)
meaning: Applies weight decay λ directly to the weights instead of adding it to the gradient, so the decay is not distorted by Adam's per-parameter scaling (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). Each step shrinks every weight by the fraction η × λ; LLM runs typically use λ = 0.1 (PyTorch's AdamW default is 0.01).
used_for: The standard optimizer for Transformers and fine-tuning (GPT-3, Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3); in 2026 frontier recipes it handles embeddings, output heads and 1-D parameters alongside Muon. In the book: Chapter 13 (AdamW: weight decay done right; the training script).

name: Lion (evolved sign momentum)
meaning: Uses only the sign (+1 or −1) of an interpolated momentum, so every parameter moves by exactly η each step; it keeps one state buffer instead of Adam's two. Found partly by automated program search (Chen et al., Google, 2023); it needs a learning rate about 3-10 times smaller and weight decay 3-10 times larger than AdamW.
used_for: A lower-memory alternative to AdamW in some Google vision, language and diffusion training. In the book: Chapter 13 (Beyond Adam: Lion, Shampoo and SOAP).

name: Muon (momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz)
formula: B ← μ × B + G ; M = G + μ × B (Nesterov) or M = B ; O = NewtonSchulz5(M) ; W ← W − η × (s × O + λ × W), with s = sqrt(max(1, rows ÷ cols)) (original) or s = 0.2 × sqrt(max(rows, cols)) (Moonshot, matches AdamW's update size)
meaning: For each 2-D weight matrix, takes the momentum of its gradient and replaces it by the nearest orthogonal matrix (if M = U × S × Vᵀ, the update is about U × Vᵀ: same directions, all strengths equal), then applies decoupled weight decay. Embeddings, the output head and 1-D parameters stay on AdamW.
used_for: Keller Jordan's NanoGPT-speedrun and CIFAR-10 records (December 2024), Moonlight (February 2025), Kimi K2 (as MuonClip), GLM-4.5, DeepSeek V4; torch.optim.Muon since PyTorch 2.9 (defaults lr 0.001, momentum 0.95, Nesterov on, weight decay 0.1). In the book: Chapter 13 (Muon: balance the whole matrix; toy 2 × 2 example).

name: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization iteration
formula: X_0 = M ÷ (sqrt(sum of all M_ij^2) + ε) ; repeat 5 times: A = X × Xᵀ, X ← a × X + (b × A + c × A × A) × X, with (a, b, c) = (3.4445, −4.7750, 2.0315) ; classic cubic form: X ← 1.5 × X − 0.5 × X × Xᵀ × X
meaning: After scaling M so its largest stretch factor is at most 1, each round of three matrix multiplications pushes every singular value toward 1 without computing an SVD; the tuned quintic coefficients get them into roughly 0.7 to 1.2 in five rounds in bfloat16. The matrix is transposed first if it has more rows than columns.
used_for: The inner loop of Muon and its 2025-26 variants; PyTorch's Muon defaults are ns_coefficients (3.4445, −4.775, 2.0315) and ns_steps 5. In the book: Chapter 13 (Muon; Newton-Schulz iteration definition).

name: Adafactor (factored second moments)
formula: for an n × m gradient G: R ← β_2t × R + (1 − β_2t) × (row sums of G^2) ; C ← β_2t × C + (1 − β_2t) × (column sums of G^2) ; V̂ = (R × C) ÷ (sum of R) (outer product) ; U = G ÷ sqrt(V̂) ; U ← U ÷ max(1, RMS(U) ÷ d), d = 1 ; β_2t = 1 − t^(−0.8) ; relative step η_t = max(ε_2, RMS(θ)) × min(10^-2, 1 ÷ sqrt(t))
meaning: Stores only a row vector and a column vector of squared-gradient averages (n + m numbers) instead of a full n × m matrix, rebuilds an approximate second moment as their outer product, clips the update's root-mean-square, and by default keeps no first moment (Shazeer and Stern, 2018).
used_for: T5 and other Google TPU training (T5X), PaLM (in an unfactored form), memory-light fine-tuning. In the book: Only here.

name: Shampoo and SOAP (Kronecker-factored preconditioning)
formula: Shampoo: L ← L + G × Gᵀ ; R ← R + Gᵀ × G ; W ← W − η × L^(−1/4) × G × R^(−1/4) ; SOAP: Q_L, Q_R = eigenvectors of L and R (refreshed every f steps), G' = Q_Lᵀ × G × Q_R, run an Adam step on G', rotate the update back as Q_L × U' × Q_Rᵀ
meaning: Shampoo (Gupta, Koren and Singer, 2018) keeps a left and a right curvature summary per weight matrix and preconditions the gradient from both sides, approximating full-matrix AdaGrad; SOAP (Vyas et al., 2024) runs Adam in Shampoo's eigenbasis. K-FAC is a related Kronecker-factored method; Muon can be read as Shampoo without the accumulation.
used_for: Distributed Shampoo won the external-tuning track of the MLCommons AlgoPerf training-speed benchmark (2024); SOAP is used in research and some large runs. In the book: Chapter 13 (Beyond Adam: Lion, Shampoo and SOAP; optimizer table).

name: Exponential moving average of weights (Polyak averaging, checkpoint averaging)
formula: θ_EMA ← β × θ_EMA + (1 − β) × θ, with β ≈ 0.999 to 0.9999 ; uniform average of K checkpoints: θ_avg = (1 ÷ K) × sum over k of θ_k
meaning: Keeps a slowly moving copy of the weights that smooths out step-to-step noise; the averaged copy, not the raw one, is evaluated or released. Stochastic weight averaging and model soups are uniform-average relatives.
used_for: Diffusion and image generators (an EMA copy is standard in Stable Diffusion-style training), DeepSeek-V3's EMA of parameters during pretraining for early quality estimates, self-distillation teachers, checkpoint averaging before release. In the book: Only here.

name: Linear learning-rate warmup
formula: η_t = η_max × t ÷ T_warmup for t < T_warmup (the book's script uses (t + 1) ÷ T_warmup)
meaning: Starts the learning rate near zero and raises it in a straight line to its peak over the first T_warmup steps, so the first chaotic steps are small while Adam's running averages are still unreliable. Book example: peak 0.001, 1,000 warmup steps, 0.0005 at step 500.
used_for: Nearly every Transformer run (Llama 3 405B used 8,000 warmup steps); also batch-size warmup in some runs. In the book: Chapter 13 (Schedules: the learning rate changes during training; training script with 50-step warmup).

name: Cosine learning-rate decay (cosine annealing)
formula: η_t = η_min + 0.5 × (η_max − η_min) × (1 + cos(π × (t − T_w) ÷ (T − T_w))) for T_w ≤ t ≤ T
meaning: After warmup, lowers the learning rate along half a cosine wave from the peak η_max to a floor η_min at the final step T: slowly at first, fastest in the middle, gently at the end. Warm restarts (SGDR) repeat the curve.
used_for: GPT-3 (decay to 10% of peak), Llama 1-3, Chinchilla, most vision recipes. Book example: 10,000 steps, peak 0.001: 0.0005 halfway through decay, about 0.00015 at three-quarters. In the book: Chapter 13 (Schedules; Figure 13.3; training script).

name: Linear, step and exponential learning-rate decay
formula: linear: η_t = η_max × (1 − t ÷ T) ; step: η = η_0 × γ^floor(epoch ÷ s) ; exponential: η_t = η_0 × γ^t ; reduce-on-plateau: η ← γ × η when validation loss stalls
meaning: The older and simpler schedules: a straight line to zero, a drop by a factor γ every s epochs (for example divide by 10 every 30 epochs), or a constant fractional decay per step.
used_for: BERT and the Hugging Face Trainer default (linear decay), 2010s ImageNet CNN recipes such as ResNet (step decay), many fine-tuning scripts. In the book: Chapter 13 (The 2026 recipe at a glance: 'divide by 10 a few times when progress stalls').

name: Warmup-stable-decay (WSD, trapezoidal) schedule
formula: η_t = η_max × t ÷ T_w for t < T_w ; η_t = η_max for T_w ≤ t < T_d ; then over the final phase either linear η_max × (T − t) ÷ (T − T_d), or 1 − sqrt: η_max × (1 − sqrt((t − T_d) ÷ (T − T_d)))
meaning: Holds the peak learning rate for most of training and decays it only in a short final phase (often the last 10-20%), so a run can be extended or branched into a finished checkpoint at any time without knowing its total length in advance. MiniCPM used an exponential decay phase; Hägele et al. (2024) recommend the 1 − sqrt shape.
used_for: MiniCPM (2024), DeepSeek-V3 (constant phase then cosine decay), Kimi K2 and many 2025-26 open runs; the decay phase is where mid-training and annealing data are fed. In the book: Chapter 13 (Schedules: WSD worked table); Chapter 19 (Mid-training and annealing).

name: Inverse square-root ('Noam') schedule
formula: η = d_model^(−0.5) × min(step^(−0.5), step × warmup^(−1.5)), warmup = 4,000 ; T5 variant: η = 1 ÷ sqrt(max(step, k)), k = 10,000
meaning: Rises linearly during warmup, then decays in proportion to 1 ÷ sqrt(step), with the peak set by the model width d_model. It needs no total-length setting.
used_for: The original 2017 Transformer, fairseq translation models and T5 pretraining; still a default in some sequence-to-sequence toolkits. In the book: Only here.

name: Learning-rate scaling with batch size (linear and square-root rules)
formula: SGD linear rule: η = η_base × B ÷ B_base (Goyal et al.: 0.1 × B ÷ 256 for ResNet-50) ; Adam square-root rule: η = η_base × sqrt(B ÷ B_base)
meaning: A bigger batch gives a less noisy gradient, so steps can be larger: proportionally for SGD (with warmup), roughly with the square root for adaptive optimizers. Both break down above a critical batch size (owned by the llm and compute categories).
used_for: Training ImageNet in one hour at batch 8,192 (2017); retuning when adding GPUs; batch-size ramps such as Llama 3 doubling its batch during training. In the book: Chapter 13 (Batch size and the learning rate).

name: Gradient clipping by global norm
formula: length(g) = sqrt(sum over all parameters i of g_i^2) ; g ← g × min(1, c ÷ length(g)) ; by value: g_i ← max(−c, min(c, g_i))
meaning: If the combined gradient of all parameters is longer than a threshold c (1.0 is typical), shrink it to length c, keeping its direction; this stops a single bad batch from throwing the weights far away. Adaptive gradient clipping (NFNets) clips relative to each weight's norm instead.
used_for: RNN training (Pascanu et al., 2013) and almost every LLM run (GPT-3, Llama 3 and DeepSeek-V3 clip at 1.0); torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_. In the book: Chapter 13 (Loss spikes; training script line clip_grad_norm_).

name: Loss scaling for 16-bit mixed-precision training
formula: L_scaled = S × L ; g = ∇L_scaled ÷ S ; dynamic rule: if any gradient is inf or NaN, skip the step and S ← 0.5 × S ; after N clean steps, S ← 2 × S
meaning: Multiplies the loss by a large factor S before backpropagation so tiny gradients do not underflow to zero in FP16, then divides it back out before the update. PyTorch's GradScaler starts at S = 65,536 and doubles every 2,000 clean steps; BF16 usually needs no scaling. Per-tensor and per-block scaling for FP8 and FP4 belong with number formats and quantization.
used_for: FP16 mixed-precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2018; NVIDIA Apex; torch.amp). In the book: Only here (Chapter 13, Numbers on hardware: precision in brief, covers mixed precision in words).

name: Batch normalization
formula: μ_B = (1 ÷ m) × sum over i of x_i ; σ_B^2 = (1 ÷ m) × sum over i of (x_i − μ_B)^2 ; x̂_i = (x_i − μ_B) ÷ sqrt(σ_B^2 + ε) ; y_i = γ × x̂_i + β ; inference statistics: μ_run ← (1 − a) × μ_run + a × μ_B (PyTorch a = 0.1)
meaning: Normalizes each feature (each channel in a CNN, pooled over positions) using the mean and variance across the m examples of the current batch, then applies a learned scale γ and shift β. At inference the running averages replace batch statistics, and the whole operation can be folded into the preceding convolution.
used_for: ResNets, EfficientNet and most CNNs since Ioffe and Szegedy (2015). In the book: Chapter 13 (The family of normalizations; Batch normalization definition).

name: Layer normalization (and group and instance normalization)
formula: μ = (1 ÷ d) × sum over i of x_i ; σ^2 = (1 ÷ d) × sum over i of (x_i − μ)^2 ; y_i = γ_i × (x_i − μ) ÷ sqrt(σ^2 + ε) + β_i
meaning: Normalizes the d features of one example (one token's vector) to mean 0 and spread 1, independent of the batch, then applies learned gain γ and shift β (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016). GroupNorm computes the same statistics over groups of channels (one group equals LayerNorm over channels and positions; one channel per group is InstanceNorm). Book example: [2, 4, 6, 8] becomes [−1.342, −0.447, 0.447, 1.342].
used_for: The original Transformer, BERT, GPT-2 and GPT-3, ViT; GroupNorm in diffusion U-Nets; InstanceNorm in style transfer. In the book: Chapter 13 (Layer normalization, worked by hand; family table).

name: RMSNorm
formula: RMS(x) = sqrt((1 ÷ d) × sum over i of x_i^2 + ε) ; y_i = g_i × x_i ÷ RMS(x)
meaning: Layer normalization without the mean subtraction or bias: divide by the root-mean-square and multiply by a learned gain g (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019); cheaper and just as effective. Gemma parameterizes the gain as (1 + g). Book example: [2, 4, 6, 8] becomes [0.365, 0.730, 1.095, 1.461].
used_for: Llama 1-4, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma and Kimi models; also used inside QK-norm and mHC. In the book: Chapter 13 (Layer normalization, worked by hand; RMSNorm definition); Chapter 15 (2017 versus 2026 table).

name: QK-norm (normalized queries and keys)
formula: q ← RMSNorm(q) ; k ← RMSNorm(k) (per head, before RoPE) ; then score = q · k ÷ sqrt(d_k), or a learned scale in place of 1 ÷ sqrt(d_k)
meaning: Normalizes each query and key vector before the dot product so attention scores cannot grow without bound, which removes a main source of loss spikes and attention-entropy collapse (Henry et al., 2020; Dehghani et al., ViT-22B, 2023).
used_for: ViT-22B, OLMo 2, Chameleon, Qwen3, and Gemma 3 (which replaced Gemma 2's attention soft-capping with QK-norm). In the book: Chapter 13 (Loss spikes: QK-norm); Chapter 17 (Keeping giants stable).

name: Dynamic Tanh (DyT), a normalization-free replacement
formula: DyT(x) = γ ⊙ tanh(α × x) + β, with a learnable scalar α (initialized around 0.5)
meaning: Replaces a LayerNorm or RMSNorm layer with an element-wise learned squash that bounds extreme values the way normalization does, without computing any statistics (Zhu, Chen, He, LeCun and Liu, CVPR 2025).
used_for: Research: matched normalized Transformers in tests on ViTs, Llama-style language models and diffusion Transformers; no confirmed frontier production use. In the book: Chapter 13 (family of normalizations; DyT definition); Chapter 17 (Keeping giants stable).

name: Dropout with inverted scaling (and stochastic depth)
formula: training: m_i ~ Bernoulli(1 − p), y_i = m_i × x_i ÷ (1 − p) ; inference: y = x ; stochastic depth (DropPath): y = x + (m ÷ (1 − p)) × F(x), one m per example
meaning: During training each unit is zeroed with probability p and the survivors are scaled up by 1 ÷ (1 − p), so the expected output is unchanged and nothing needs rescaling at test time. Stochastic depth drops whole residual branches instead of single units. Book example: [4, 2, 6, 8] with p = 0.5, keeping the first and third, gives [8, 0, 12, 0].
used_for: AlexNet, the original Transformer (p = 0.1), BERT; LoRA fine-tuning dropout; DropPath in ViT, DeiT and ConvNeXt; usually turned off in single-epoch LLM pretraining. In the book: Chapter 13 (The regularization toolkit: dropout worked example).

name: Weight decay and L2 (and L1) regularization
formula: L2 penalty: L_total = L + (λ ÷ 2) × sum over i of θ_i^2, giving gradient g + λ × θ ; decay step: θ ← (1 − η × λ) × θ − η × g ; L1 penalty: λ × sum over i of |θ_i|
meaning: Penalizes large weights (a small tax on complexity) by shrinking every weight a little each step. For plain SGD the L2 penalty and the decay step are identical; for Adam they differ, which is why AdamW applies decay separately. L1 pushes weights exactly to zero. Biases and normalization gains are usually exempt.
used_for: Almost all training; LLMs typically use λ = 0.1 with AdamW or Muon. In the book: Chapter 13 (The regularization toolkit; AdamW: weight decay done right).

name: Early stopping
formula: θ* = the parameters at the evaluation with the lowest validation loss ; stop when validation loss has not improved by more than δ for 'patience' evaluations
meaning: Treats the number of training steps as a hyperparameter chosen on held-out data. For gradient descent on a quadratic loss it acts like L2 regularization with strength about 1 ÷ (η × t) (Goodfellow et al., section 7.8).
used_for: Small and medium supervised models, fine-tuning runs and checkpoint selection. In the book: Chapter 13 (The regularization toolkit: early stopping).

name: Mixup and CutMix augmentation
formula: Mixup: x̃ = λ × x_i + (1 − λ) × x_j ; ỹ = λ × y_i + (1 − λ) × y_j ; λ ~ Beta(α, α) ; CutMix: x̃ = M ⊙ x_A + (1 − M) ⊙ x_B, with λ = the fraction of area kept from x_A
meaning: Trains on blends of two examples with correspondingly blended labels (Mixup), or pastes a rectangle M of one image into another (CutMix), which regularizes the classifier and calibrates its confidence. α around 0.2 to 1 controls how strong the mixing is.
used_for: Image-classifier training recipes (DeiT, ConvNeXt, the timm library), audio classification. In the book: Only here (Chapter 13 covers data augmentation in words).

name: Residual (skip) connection
formula: y = x + F(x) ; with a shape change: y = W_s × x + F(x) ; gradient: ∂y ÷ ∂x = I + ∂F ÷ ∂x
meaning: The layer learns only a correction F(x) that is added to its unchanged input. The identity term I in the gradient gives backpropagated signals a direct highway through hundreds of layers (He et al., 2015).
used_for: ResNet, U-Net, every Transformer's residual stream, Mamba and other sequence blocks. In the book: Chapter 13 (Residual connections: the express elevator; The residual stream in your chatbot); Chapter 14 (ResNet, 2015); Chapter 15 (Step 7).

name: Hyper-connections and manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC)
formula: with n parallel residual streams x_l (shape n × C): x_(l+1) = H_res × x_l + H_postᵀ × F(H_pre × x_l) ; mHC: H_pre = sigmoid(H̃_pre), H_post = 2 × sigmoid(H̃_post), H_res = SinkhornKnopp(H̃_res): M = exp(H̃_res), then alternately divide every row and every column by its sum, 20 rounds
meaning: Hyper-connections (Zhu et al., 2024) widen the single residual stream into n streams (n = 4 in DeepSeek's experiments) with learned read-in (H_pre), write-out (H_post) and stream-mixing (H_res) weights computed from an RMSNorm of the input. mHC (DeepSeek, arXiv 2512.24880, December 2025) forces H_res to be approximately doubly stochastic (rows and columns each sum to 1), so mixing is a blend that cannot amplify signals across many layers.
used_for: DeepSeek V4 (2026). In the book: Chapter 13 (Hyper-connections and mHC definition; 2026 recipe table); Chapter 17 (Keeping giants stable: hyper-connections and mHC).

name: Convolution layer (cross-correlation of an input with learned filters)
formula: Y[o, i, j] = b_o + sum over input channels c, and u, v from 0 to k − 1, of X[c, i × s + u, j × s + v] × K[o, c, u, v]
meaning: Each output channel o slides its own k × k filter (looking through all input channels) across the input with stride s, taking a weighted sum at every position: weight sharing and local connections give translation equivariance with few parameters. Deep-learning convolution does not flip the kernel (true convolution does); 1-D versions handle audio and text, 3-D versions video.
used_for: CNNs from LeNet and AlexNet to ResNet, U-Net, YOLO and ConvNeXt; the patch embedding of Vision Transformers (stride equal to kernel size); the short causal 1-D convolutions inside Mamba and Gated DeltaNet layers. In the book: Chapter 14 (Convolution: a small flashlight; Working one convolution by hand; Channels in, channels out; Beyond flat pictures).

name: Convolution and pooling output size (padding, stride, dilation, transposed convolution)
formula: n_out = floor((n_in + 2 × p − d × (k − 1) − 1) ÷ s) + 1, which for dilation d = 1 is floor((n_in + 2 × p − k) ÷ s) + 1 ; 'same' padding for odd k and s = 1: p = (k − 1) ÷ 2 ; transposed convolution: n_out = (n_in − 1) × s − 2 × p + d × (k − 1) + output_padding + 1
meaning: Gives the output width (and separately height) from input size n_in, kernel size k, padding p, stride s and dilation d. Book example: (224 − 3 + 2) ÷ 2 + 1 = 112.5, rounded down to 112. Transposed (up-sampling) convolutions run the formula in reverse.
used_for: Designing every CNN, U-Net decoder and ViT patchifier; the same formula sizes pooling layers. In the book: Chapter 14 (Stride and padding: how the flashlight moves).

name: Convolution parameter count and cost (including depthwise separable)
formula: parameters = (k_h × k_w × C_in ÷ groups + 1) × C_out ; multiply-adds = H_out × W_out × k_h × k_w × (C_in ÷ groups) × C_out ; depthwise separable: k^2 × C_in + C_in × C_out weights, versus k^2 × C_in × C_out for a standard convolution
meaning: A filter's weights are shared over every position, so the count depends on kernel size and channels, not image size; the cost scales with the output area. Splitting a convolution into a per-channel (depthwise) step and a 1 × 1 (pointwise) step cuts weights and compute by roughly 1 ÷ C_out + 1 ÷ k^2.
used_for: Sizing CNNs; MobileNet, Xception and EfficientNet are built on depthwise separable convolutions. In the book: Chapter 14 (Channels in, channels out; The big trick: the same filter everywhere; After ResNet: smaller, faster CNNs).

name: Receptive field of stacked convolutions
formula: r_l = r_(l−1) + (k_l − 1) × j_(l−1) ; j_l = j_(l−1) × s_l ; starting from r_0 = 1, j_0 = 1
meaning: r_l is how many input pixels (per side) one unit in layer l can see and j_l is the jump, the product of all earlier strides. Three stacked 3 × 3 stride-1 layers see 3, 5 and 7 pixels; strides and pooling make it grow much faster, and dilation uses the effective kernel size d × (k − 1) + 1.
used_for: Designing detection and segmentation networks, WaveNet-style dilated stacks, and explaining the feature hierarchy of CNNs. In the book: Chapter 14 (Receptive fields and the feature hierarchy).

name: Max, average and global average pooling
formula: max pooling: Y[i, j] = max over (u, v) in the window of X[i × s + u, j × s + v] ; average pooling: mean over the window ; global average pooling: y_c = (1 ÷ (H × W)) × sum over i, j of X[c, i, j]
meaning: Summarizes each small window by its largest value or its mean, shrinking the map and adding tolerance to small shifts; in backpropagation max pooling sends the gradient only to the winning position. Global average pooling collapses each channel to one number (squeeze-and-excitation blocks use it to compute channel gates).
used_for: Down-sampling in LeNet, VGG and ResNet stems; global average pooling before classifier heads in ResNet and EfficientNet; mean pooling of token vectors for sentence embeddings. In the book: Chapter 14 (Pooling: making a thumbnail, 2 × 2 worked example).

name: Recurrent neural network update (Elman RNN)
formula: h_t = tanh(W_hh × h_(t−1) + W_xh × x_t + b_h) ; y_t = W_hy × h_t + b_y
meaning: A fixed-size hidden state h_t is updated from the previous state and the current input with the same weights at every time step (unrolling the loop gives a deep network with shared weights). Bidirectional RNNs run a second pass backward and join the two states.
used_for: Pre-2017 language models, speech recognition and translation encoders; the ancestor of state-space models and linear attention. In the book: Chapter 14 (Recurrent neural networks: reading with a running memory; Unrolling the loop; A worked example: watching memory fade).

name: LSTM gates and cell update
formula: f_t = sigmoid(W_f × [h_(t−1), x_t] + b_f) ; i_t = sigmoid(W_i × [h_(t−1), x_t] + b_i) ; o_t = sigmoid(W_o × [h_(t−1), x_t] + b_o) ; c̃_t = tanh(W_c × [h_(t−1), x_t] + b_c) ; c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ c̃_t ; h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)
meaning: [a, b] joins two vectors end to end. The forget gate f, input gate i and output gate o are valves between 0 and 1; the cell state c changes mainly by gated addition, so information and gradients survive long sequences (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; forget gate by Gers et al., 2000). The forget-gate bias is often initialized to 1. xLSTM (2024) uses exponential gates and a matrix memory.
used_for: Google's neural machine translation (2016), 2015-2019 speech recognition, ELMo, AlphaStar; xLSTM 7B (2025). In the book: Chapter 14 (LSTM and GRU: memory with valves; A worked example with the gates); Chapter 17 (RWKV and xLSTM).

name: GRU (gated recurrent unit)
formula: z_t = sigmoid(W_z × x_t + U_z × h_(t−1) + b_z) ; r_t = sigmoid(W_r × x_t + U_r × h_(t−1) + b_r) ; h̃_t = tanh(W_h × x_t + U_h × (r_t ⊙ h_(t−1)) + b_h) ; h_t = (1 − z_t) ⊙ h_(t−1) + z_t ⊙ h̃_t
meaning: A lighter LSTM with two gates and no separate cell: the update gate z blends old state and new candidate, the reset gate r decides how much of the old state the candidate may use (Cho et al., 2014, who write the last line with z and 1 − z swapped; libraries differ).
used_for: Speech, time-series and on-device sequence models; research revivals such as minGRU (2024). In the book: Chapter 14 (LSTM and GRU: memory with valves).

name: Additive (Bahdanau) and multiplicative (Luong) attention
formula: e_ij = v_aᵀ × tanh(W_a × s_(i−1) + U_a × h_j) ; α_ij = exp(e_ij) ÷ sum over k of exp(e_ik) ; c_i = sum over j of α_ij × h_j ; Luong scores: s_iᵀ × h_j (dot) or s_iᵀ × W_a × h_j (general)
meaning: The decoder state s scores every encoder state h_j with a small network (or a dot product), softmax turns the scores into weights α_ij, and the context vector c_i is the weighted average of encoder states, removing the fixed-size bottleneck of sequence-to-sequence models (Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, 2014; Luong et al., 2015).
used_for: Neural machine translation 2015-2017 (including Google's 2016 system), Listen-Attend-Spell speech recognition; the direct ancestor of Transformer attention. In the book: Chapter 14 (Sequence to sequence: translation and its bottleneck; The birth of attention).

name: Scaled dot-product attention
formula: Q = X × W_Q, K = X × W_K, V = X × W_V ; Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q × Kᵀ ÷ sqrt(d_k) + M) × V (softmax along each row)
meaning: Each token's query is compared with every key by a dot product, the scores are divided by sqrt(d_k) (a dot product of d_k unit-variance numbers has variance d_k, so this keeps scores near unit size), a mask M blocks forbidden pairs, softmax makes weights, and the output is the weighted sum of values. In cross-attention Q comes from one sequence and K, V from another.
used_for: Every Transformer (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, ViT, Whisper, diffusion Transformers); PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention; FlashAttention computes it exactly in tiles (owned by llm). In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 4: Self-attention, worked by hand, Steps A to E); Chapter 17 (Two bills every Transformer pays).

name: Attention masks (causal, padding, sliding-window, document and prefix)
formula: M_ij = 0 if token i may attend to token j, else −∞ (added to the scores before softmax) ; causal: allowed if j ≤ i ; sliding window of W tokens: allowed if i − W < j ≤ i ; document mask for packed sequences: allowed if j ≤ i and i, j are in the same document ; prefix-LM: every token sees the whole prefix
meaning: Because exp(−∞) = 0, masked pairs get exactly zero attention weight. The causal mask makes a model predict each token from earlier ones only; padding masks hide filler tokens; sliding windows cap how far back a layer looks, so its cache stops growing.
used_for: The causal mask in every decoder-only LLM; BERT's bidirectional attention with a padding mask; sliding windows in Mistral 7B (4,096 tokens), Gemma 3 (five 1,024-token local layers per global layer) and gpt-oss (alternating 128-token banded and full layers); document masking in Llama 3 pretraining. In the book: Chapter 15 (The whole attention matrix, with the mask; Step 8: Encoders, decoders and the causal mask; Making attention cheaper).

name: Multi-head attention with output projection
formula: head_h = Attention(X × W_Q^h, X × W_K^h, X × W_V^h) for h = 1..H, each of size d_head = d_model ÷ H ; MHA(X) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_H) × W_O ; parameters ≈ 4 × d_model^2
meaning: Runs H smaller attention calculations side by side, each free to track a different relationship, joins their outputs and mixes them with the output matrix W_O. Book example: GPT-2 small has 12 heads of 64 numbers (768 total) and 4 × 768 × 768 ≈ 2.36 million attention weights per layer.
used_for: Every Transformer layer; the head is the unit studied in interpretability (induction heads). In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 5: Many heads, and how to save their memory).

name: Multi-query and grouped-query attention (MQA, GQA)
formula: H query heads share G key-value heads: query head h (counting from 0) uses key-value head g = floor(h ÷ (H ÷ G)) ; G = H is ordinary multi-head attention, G = 1 is multi-query attention ; key-value storage shrinks by the factor H ÷ G
meaning: Several query heads read the same keys and values, cutting the KV cache and memory traffic during generation with little quality loss (MQA: Shazeer, 2019; GQA: Ainslie et al., 2023). The KV-cache size formula itself is owned by the llm category.
used_for: PaLM (MQA); Llama 2 70B and Llama 3 (8 KV heads), Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss; about 65% of the 111 models in Sebastian Raschka's 2026 architecture survey. In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 5; The KV cache and its memory bill); Chapter 23; Chapter 33.

name: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
formula: c_KV = W_DKV × h_t ; k_C = W_UK × c_KV ; v_C = W_UV × c_KV ; k_R = RoPE(W_KR × h_t), shared by all heads ; key of head i = [k_C,i ; k_R] ; queries: c_Q = W_DQ × h_t, q_C = W_UQ × c_Q, q_R = RoPE(W_QR × c_Q) ; cache only c_KV and k_R per token per layer
meaning: Keys and values are compressed into one small latent vector c_KV that is cached instead of full per-head keys and values; a separate small decoupled RoPE key carries position because RoPE would block folding W_UK into the query side at inference (W_UV likewise folds into W_O). DeepSeek-V3 uses a latent of 512 plus a RoPE key of 64, so 576 numbers per token per layer.
used_for: DeepSeek-V2, V3 and R1; Kimi K2 and Kimi K3 (gated MLA, per the book); the full-attention layers of Kimi Linear; about 23% of models in Raschka's 2026 survey. In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 5); Chapter 17; Chapter 23; Chapter 33.

name: Attention with a learned sink logit (off-by-one softmax)
formula: a_ij = exp(s_ij) ÷ (exp(s_sink,h) + sum over k of exp(s_ik)) ; with s_sink = 0 this is the off-by-one softmax exp(s_ij) ÷ (1 + sum over k of exp(s_ik))
meaning: Adds a learned per-head score s_sink to the softmax denominator so a head's weights may add up to less than 1, letting it attend to nothing instead of dumping spare attention on the first token (the attention-sink effect). StreamingLLM's alternative keeps the first few tokens' keys and values permanently in the cache.
used_for: OpenAI's gpt-oss models (August 2025) use a learned per-head sink bias; StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) for unbounded streaming generation. In the book: Chapter 15 (Making attention cheaper: attention sink definition); Chapter 17 (Gated attention and attention sinks).

name: Gated attention (per-head sigmoid output gate)
formula: Y' = Y ⊙ sigmoid(X × W_θ), where Y is each head's attention output before the output projection W_O
meaning: A head-specific, element-wise sigmoid valve computed from the normalized hidden state X can turn each head's output down, adding non-linearity and sparsity; it removes attention sinks and massive activations and improves training stability (Qiu et al., Qwen team, arXiv 2505.06708, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper).
used_for: The full-attention layers of Qwen3-Next (September 2025) and Qwen3.5 (February 2026); gated MLA in Kimi K3 (per the book). In the book: Chapter 15 (Making attention cheaper: gated attention definition); Chapter 17 (Hybrid architectures; Keeping giants stable).

name: Top-k sparse attention with a lightning indexer (DeepSeek Sparse Attention)
formula: I_(t,s) = sum over j = 1..H_I of w_(t,j) × ReLU(q_(t,j) · k_s) ; u_t = Attention(h_t, {c_s : I_(t,s) is among the top-k of I_(t,:)}), k = 2,048
meaning: A tiny, cheap set of indexer heads (H_I heads with weights w_(t,j)) scores every earlier token s for query token t; full attention then runs only over the 2,048 highest-scoring key-value entries, so per-token cost stops growing with context length. Native Sparse Attention (DeepSeek, 2025) is a related block-selection design.
used_for: DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp (September 2025) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (arXiv 2512.02556); DeepSeek V4's Compressed Sparse Attention builds on compressed and sparse selection (V4-Pro reports 27% of V3.2's per-token compute and 10% of its KV cache at 1 million tokens). In the book: Chapter 15 (Making attention cheaper: sparse attention definition); Chapter 17 (The memory problem).

name: Pre-norm Transformer block (with post-norm, sandwich and parallel variants)
formula: pre-norm: h = x + Attention(Norm(x)) ; y = h + FFN(Norm(h)) ; post-norm (2017): h = LayerNorm(x + Attention(x)), y = LayerNorm(h + FFN(h)) ; sandwich: h = x + Norm(Attention(Norm(x))) ; parallel: y = x + Attention(Norm(x)) + FFN(Norm(x))
meaning: Each block reads a normalized copy of the residual stream, computes attention and then a feed-forward (or MoE) update, and adds each result back to the stream. Pre-norm trains stably in deep stacks; post-norm needs careful warmup; Gemma 2 and 3 normalize both before and after each sub-layer; OLMo 2 normalizes only the sub-layer outputs; GPT-J and PaLM run attention and FFN in parallel. A final norm precedes the unembedding.
used_for: GPT-2 onward; nearly every 2026 LLM is a pre-norm RMSNorm stack. In the book: Chapter 13 (Pre-norm and post-norm definition); Chapter 15 (Step 7: The residual stream and one full block).

name: Transformer feed-forward block and its width (classic and SwiGLU)
formula: classic: FFN(x) = W_2 × f(W_1 × x + b_1) + b_2, with d_ff = 4 × d_model and about 8 × d_model^2 weights ; SwiGLU: FFN(x) = W_2 × (SiLU(W_1 × x) ⊙ (W_3 × x)), with d_ff ≈ (8 ÷ 3) × d_model (rounded) to keep about 8 × d_model^2 weights
meaning: A two-layer MLP applied to each token separately: expand, bend, shrink back. The gated version has three matrices, so its hidden width is cut to about two-thirds to keep the same parameter count. Book example: GPT-2 small expands 768 to 3,072, about 4.7 million weights per layer.
used_for: Every Transformer layer (roughly two-thirds of a dense model's parameters); replaced by mixture-of-experts layers in most 2026 frontier models. In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 6: The feed-forward block, where each token thinks alone).

name: Absolute position encodings (sinusoidal and learned)
formula: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos ÷ 10000^(2i ÷ d)) ; PE(pos, 2i + 1) = cos(pos ÷ 10000^(2i ÷ d)) ; input x = E[token] + PE(pos) ; learned version: x = E[token] + P[pos]
meaning: Gives every position a unique pattern of sine and cosine waves of geometrically spaced speeds (a barcode) that is added to the token embedding; the learned version uses a trainable table P with a fixed maximum length, so the model cannot go past it.
used_for: The original 2017 Transformer (sinusoidal); BERT (512 learned positions), GPT-2 (1,024) and ViT (learned); sinusoidal timestep embeddings in diffusion models. In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 3: Telling the model about word order).

name: Rotary position embedding (RoPE)
formula: θ_i = base^(−2i ÷ d) ; for each pair (x_2i, x_2i+1) of a query or key at position m: x'_2i = x_2i × cos(m × θ_i) − x_2i+1 × sin(m × θ_i) ; x'_2i+1 = x_2i × sin(m × θ_i) + x_2i+1 × cos(m × θ_i) ; property: RoPE(q, m) · RoPE(k, n) depends only on m − n
meaning: Rotates each 2-number slice of the query and key by an angle proportional to the token's position, with a different speed θ_i per slice, so attention scores depend on relative distance. base = 10,000 originally (Su et al., 2021), 500,000 in Llama 3. Variants: pairing dimension i with i + d ÷ 2 instead of neighbors (GPT-NeoX style), partial RoPE on some dimensions, decoupled RoPE in MLA, and NoPE layers with no position signal (interleaved in Llama 4). Context extension (position interpolation, NTK, YaRN) is owned by the llm category.
used_for: Nearly every major open model: Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma, gpt-oss, Kimi. In the book: Chapter 15 (RoPE: rotating the arrows; Stretching the context window).

name: ALiBi and relative position biases
formula: score_ij = q_i · k_j ÷ sqrt(d_k) − m_h × (i − j) ; head slopes m_h = 2^(−8 × h ÷ H) for h = 1..H ; T5: score_ij + b_h(bucket(i − j)), a learned scalar per head and distance bucket
meaning: Instead of changing the token vectors, adds a penalty to each attention score that grows linearly with distance, with a different slope per head (for 8 heads: 1/2, 1/4, ..., 1/256), which lets models run on longer texts than they were trained on (Press et al., 2022). T5's relative bias learns the penalty per distance bucket.
used_for: BLOOM (176B), MPT; T5 and its descendants (bucketed relative bias). In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 3; ALiBi in key terms).

name: Embedding lookup (one-hot times a table)
formula: e = E[id] = one_hot(id)ᵀ × E, with E of shape V × d ; optional scaling e × sqrt(d)
meaning: Each token or category ID selects one row of a learned V × d table, which is mathematically the same as multiplying a one-hot vector by the table; only the selected rows receive gradient. The original Transformer and Gemma multiply the embedding by sqrt(d).
used_for: The first layer of every LLM (vocabularies of about 100,000 to 260,000 tokens), ID embeddings in recommenders, categorical features. In the book: Chapter 14 (One-hot vectors; Dense embeddings); Chapter 15 (Step 2: Token embeddings); Appendix B (Embedding table size).

name: Tied input and output embeddings (weight tying)
formula: logits = h_final × Eᵀ (the unembedding matrix is the transposed embedding table E, shape d × V)
meaning: Reuses the input embedding table as the output layer that scores every vocabulary token, saving V × d parameters (100,000 × 4,096 ≈ 410 million) and tying the meaning of reading and writing a token (Press and Wolf, 2017).
used_for: The original Transformer, GPT-2, the Gemma family and small models such as Llama 3.2 1B and 3B; most large frontier models keep separate input and output tables. In the book: Chapter 15 (Step 9: unembedding definition, weight tying).

name: word2vec skip-gram (softmax and negative sampling)
formula: P(o given c) = exp(u_o · v_c) ÷ sum over all words w of exp(u_w · v_c) ; negative sampling loss: L = −ln(sigmoid(u_o · v_c)) − sum over k = 1..K of ln(sigmoid(−u_(n_k) · v_c)) ; noise distribution P_n(w) ∝ count(w)^(3/4) ; subsampling: P(discard w) = 1 − sqrt(t ÷ f(w)), t ≈ 10^-5
meaning: Each word has a center vector v and a context vector u; training pushes the dot product up for words that really appear nearby and, with negative sampling, down for K randomly drawn noise words (K = 5 to 20 for small data, 2 to 5 for large), avoiding the full-vocabulary softmax. CBOW predicts the center from the averaged context instead (Mikolov et al., 2013).
used_for: word2vec and fastText embeddings; node2vec and DeepWalk graph embeddings; item2vec-style recommender embeddings; the negative-sampling idea recurs throughout contrastive training. In the book: Chapter 14 (word2vec: learning meaning from neighbors).

name: GloVe objective
formula: J = sum over i, j of f(X_ij) × (w_i · w̃_j + b_i + b̃_j − ln(X_ij))^2 ; f(x) = (x ÷ x_max)^(3/4) if x < x_max, else 1 ; x_max = 100
meaning: Fits word vectors w and context vectors w̃ (with biases b) so that their dot product matches the log of how often the two words co-occur (X_ij), weighting frequent pairs more but capping the weight at 1 (Pennington, Socher and Manning, 2014).
used_for: The GloVe pretrained vectors (Stanford, 2014), widely used before contextual embeddings; a standard CS224n topic. In the book: Chapter 14 (mentions Stanford's GloVe, 2014).

name: Mixture-of-experts router, top-k gating and layer output (with shared experts)
formula: s = softmax(W_r × x) (or s_i = sigmoid(x · e_i) in DeepSeek-V3) ; T = indices of the k largest s_i ; g_i = s_i ÷ sum over j in T of s_j for i in T, else 0 ; MoE(x) = sum over shared experts j of E_j(x) + sum over i in T of g_i × E_i(x)
meaning: A small router scores every expert for each token, keeps the top k, renormalizes their scores into gating weights (some models skip renormalization) and returns the weighted sum of those experts' outputs plus any always-on shared experts; the result is added to the residual stream. Expert-choice routing flips it: each expert picks its top tokens.
used_for: Switch Transformer (k = 1), Mixtral (8 experts, k = 2), DeepSeek-V3 (256 routed plus 1 shared, k = 8), Kimi K2 (384 experts, 8 active plus 1 shared), Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, gpt-oss, Llama 4, Mistral Large 3, Kimi K3 (896 experts, 16 routed plus 2 shared per the book). In the book: Chapter 17 (Worked example: routing one token; Shared experts and fine-grained experts); Chapter 15 (Step 6); Appendix B (Mixture of experts).

name: MoE load-balancing auxiliary loss
formula: L_aux = α × N × sum over i = 1..N of f_i × P_i ; f_i = fraction of the batch's tokens sent to expert i ; P_i = (1 ÷ T) × sum over the T tokens of s_i(x)
meaning: Multiplies each expert's share of tokens by its average router probability; the sum is smallest (equal to α) when both are uniform at 1 ÷ N, so the penalty pushes the router toward even use and prevents routing collapse. Switch used α = 0.01; DeepSeek-V3 keeps only a tiny per-sequence version (α = 0.0001) and Qwen3 computes it over the global batch.
used_for: GShard, Switch Transformer, Mixtral-era MoEs, DeepSeek-V2, Qwen MoEs. In the book: Chapter 17 (Load balancing: auxiliary loss).

name: Router z-loss
formula: L_z = c_z × (1 ÷ B) × sum over the B tokens of (ln(sum over j of exp(r_j)))^2, with c_z = 0.001
meaning: Penalizes large router logits r_j (through the squared log of their softmax normalizer), keeping the router's numbers small enough for stable bfloat16 arithmetic without hurting quality (Zoph et al., ST-MoE, 2022).
used_for: ST-MoE, OLMoE and many open MoE training recipes. In the book: Only here.

name: Auxiliary-loss-free bias balancing
formula: T = indices of the k largest (s_i + b_i) ; gating weights still use s_i: g_i = s_i ÷ sum over j in T of s_j ; after each step: b_i ← b_i + γ × sign(mean load − load_i)
meaning: A per-expert bias b_i is added to router scores only when choosing experts; overloaded experts get their bias lowered by γ and underused ones raised, balancing load without a loss term that fights the language-modeling objective (Wang et al., 2024). DeepSeek-V3 used γ = 0.001 for its first 14.3 trillion tokens, then 0. Book example: scores 2.0, 1.3, 1.1 with biases −0.5, 0, +0.5 select experts E8 and E3.
used_for: DeepSeek-V3, R1 and V3.2 and other 2025-26 MoEs. In the book: Chapter 17 (Load balancing: auxiliary-loss-free balancing worked example).

name: Expert capacity (capacity factor)
formula: capacity = ceiling(capacity_factor × tokens_per_batch × k ÷ N_experts)
meaning: The most tokens one expert accepts per batch; tokens beyond it are dropped from that expert and pass through on the residual stream. Book example: 16 tokens × top-2 ÷ 8 experts = 4 fair share, × 1.25 = 5. Dropless MoE implementations (for example MegaBlocks) avoid the cap.
used_for: GShard, Switch Transformer (capacity factor 1.0 to 1.25 in training) and other static-shape TPU MoEs; expert-parallel serving systems. In the book: Chapter 17 (Load balancing: expert capacity; Figure 17.4).

name: Linear state-space model layer (continuous, discrete and convolution forms)
formula: continuous: h'(t) = A × h(t) + B × x(t), y(t) = C × h(t) + D × x(t) ; discrete recurrence: h_t = Ā × h_(t−1) + B̄ × x_t, y_t = C × h_t + D × x_t ; convolution form (S4): K̄ = (C × B̄, C × Ā × B̄, C × Ā^2 × B̄, ..., C × Ā^(L−1) × B̄), y = K̄ * x
meaning: A fixed-size state h is updated by a linear recurrence from control engineering and read out through C (D is a skip term). When A, B, C are the same for every token the whole recurrence equals one long causal convolution with kernel K̄, so training is parallel (via FFT) while generation is a constant-memory recurrence. The classical linear-Gaussian state-space model and Kalman filter are owned by generative-classical.
used_for: S4 (2021), H3 and other pre-Mamba long-sequence models; the base of the Mamba family. Book toy: state = 0.9 × state + input. In the book: Chapter 17 (Back to recurrence, done right; From S4 to Mamba-3).

name: SSM discretization (zero-order hold, Euler, exponential-trapezoidal)
formula: zero-order hold: Ā = exp(Δ × A), B̄ = (Δ × A)^(−1) × (exp(Δ × A) − I) × Δ × B ; Mamba's simplification: B̄ ≈ Δ × B ; Mamba-3: h_t = α_t × h_(t−1) + β_t × B_(t−1) × x_(t−1) + γ_t × B_t × x_t, with α_t = exp(Δ_t × A_t), β_t = (1 − λ_t) × Δ_t × α_t, γ_t = λ_t × Δ_t
meaning: Converts the continuous equations into a per-token update using a step size Δ. Mamba-3's exponential-trapezoidal rule blends the previous and current inputs with a data-dependent λ_t between 0 and 1 (λ_t = 1/2 is the classical trapezoid rule; λ_t = 1 recovers Mamba-2's Euler-style update).
used_for: S4 and Mamba (zero-order hold), Mamba-2 (Euler-style), Mamba-3 (Lahoti et al., arXiv 2603.15569, March 2026; ICLR 2026). In the book: Chapter 17 (From S4 to Mamba-3).

name: Mamba selective scan
formula: Δ_t = softplus(W_Δ × x_t + b_Δ) ; B_t = W_B × x_t ; C_t = W_C × x_t ; h_t = exp(Δ_t × A) ⊙ h_(t−1) + Δ_t × B_t × x_t ; y_t = C_t · h_t + D × x_t
meaning: Makes the step size Δ and the read/write vectors B and C depend on the current token, so the layer can choose what to keep and what to forget (selectivity); A is diagonal and learned. Because the update is no longer a fixed convolution, training uses a hardware-aware parallel scan. A Mamba block wraps the scan with an input projection, a short causal convolution, SiLU and a SiLU-gated output (Gu and Dao, December 2023).
used_for: Mamba, Jamba (AI21), Falcon Mamba, Codestral Mamba. In the book: Chapter 17 (Back to recurrence: selectivity; From S4 to Mamba-3).

name: Mamba-2 state-space duality (scalar-decay SSM as masked attention)
formula: h_t = a_t × h_(t−1) + B_t × x_tᵀ, y_t = h_tᵀ × C_t, with a scalar a_t = exp(Δ_t × A) per head ; matrix form: y = (L ⊙ (C × Bᵀ)) × x, where L_ij = a_i × a_(i−1) × ... × a_(j+1) for i ≥ j and 0 otherwise
meaning: Restricting A to a scalar times the identity makes the whole layer equal to attention without softmax, with a causal mask L of cumulative decays; computing it in chunks turns most of the work into matrix multiplications, which made training several times faster (Dao and Gu, 2024).
used_for: Mamba-2 layers in NVIDIA's Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3 Nano and Super, IBM Granite 4.0 and Falcon-H1 hybrids. In the book: Chapter 17 (From S4 to Mamba-3: Mamba-2; Hybrid architectures table).

name: Linear attention and its recurrent form (with decay gates)
formula: o_i = (φ(q_i)ᵀ × sum over j ≤ i of φ(k_j) × v_jᵀ) ÷ (φ(q_i)ᵀ × sum over j ≤ i of φ(k_j)) ; recurrent: S_t = S_(t−1) + v_t × φ(k_t)ᵀ, o_t = S_t × φ(q_t) ; decayed: S_t = γ × S_(t−1) + v_t × k_tᵀ (RetNet) ; data-dependent gate: S_t = G_t ⊙ S_(t−1) + v_t × k_tᵀ (GLA)
meaning: Replacing softmax with a feature map φ (for example elu(x) + 1, Katharopoulos et al., 2020) lets the sum over the past be folded into one fixed-size memory matrix S, so each new token costs the same no matter how long the text is; many modern versions drop the normalizer. Decay γ or a learned gate G_t lets old memories fade; Mamba-2 is the scalar-gate case.
used_for: MiniMax-01's lightning attention (seven linear layers per softmax layer), RetNet, RWKV-style models; the base of delta-rule layers. Book worked example: write value × keyᵀ, read S × q. In the book: Chapter 17 (Linear attention and the delta rule); Chapter 15 (Making attention cheaper).

name: Delta rule, Gated DeltaNet and Kimi Delta Attention
formula: DeltaNet: S_t = S_(t−1) − β_t × (S_(t−1) × k_t − v_t) × k_tᵀ = S_(t−1) × (I − β_t × k_t × k_tᵀ) + β_t × v_t × k_tᵀ ; Gated DeltaNet: S_t = α_t × S_(t−1) × (I − β_t × k_t × k_tᵀ) + β_t × v_t × k_tᵀ ; Kimi Delta Attention: S_t = S_(t−1) × Diag(α_t) × (I − β_t × k_t × k_tᵀ) + β_t × v_t × k_tᵀ ; read-out o_t = S_t × q_t
meaning: Before writing, the memory is asked what it returns for key k_t, and only the difference from the new value v_t is written, with strength β_t between 0 and 1 (one step of online least squares, the Widrow-Hoff rule); keys are length-normalized. Gated DeltaNet adds a scalar forget gate α_t (Yang et al., ICLR 2025); KDA gives every key channel its own gate (Kimi Linear paper, arXiv 2510.26692, written there in the transposed convention).
used_for: Qwen3-Next (September 2025, 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per gated-attention layer) and Qwen3.5 (February 2026); Kimi Linear (October 2025, 3 KDA layers per MLA layer) and Kimi K3 (69 KDA and 24 gated MLA layers, per the book). Book worked example: storing [3, 1] then [2, 2] under key [1, 0]. In the book: Chapter 17 (Linear attention and the delta rule; Gated DeltaNet and KDA definitions; Hybrid architectures).

name: Output z-loss
formula: L_z = c × (ln(Z))^2, with Z = sum over the vocabulary of exp(z_j) and c = 10^-4
meaning: An extra loss term that pushes the log of the softmax normalizer toward 0, so the output logits cannot drift to huge values that break low-precision arithmetic; it does not change which token is most likely.
used_for: PaLM (2022), Chameleon, OLMo 2. In the book: Only here.

name: Logit soft-capping
formula: capped = cap × tanh(logits ÷ cap)
meaning: A smooth limiter: values well below the cap pass almost unchanged, large values saturate near plus or minus cap, and gradients stay defined. Gemma 2 used cap = 50 for attention scores and cap = 30 for the final logits.
used_for: Gemma 2 (2024) and Grok-1 (open weights, 2024, attention logits capped at 30); Gemma 3 dropped the attention soft-cap in favor of QK-norm. In the book: Only here.

name: QK-Clip (the 'clip' in MuonClip)
formula: S_max^h = (1 ÷ sqrt(d)) × max over the batch's tokens i, j of q_i^h · k_j^h ; γ_h = min(1, τ ÷ S_max^h), τ = 100 ; if S_max^h > τ: W_q^h ← sqrt(γ_h) × W_q^h and W_k^h ← sqrt(γ_h) × W_k^h ; for MLA: content query and key weights × sqrt(γ_h), head-specific rotary query × γ_h, shared rotary key untouched
meaning: After each optimizer step, any attention head whose largest score exceeded the threshold τ has its query and key weights shrunk so that score would land back at τ; it rescales weights rather than clipping logits and leaves all other heads alone.
used_for: Kimi K2 (July 2025; Moonshot report arXiv 2507.20534) pretrained on 15.5 trillion tokens with Muon plus QK-Clip and reported zero loss spikes. In the book: Chapter 13 (Muon: MuonClip; Loss spikes); Chapter 17 (stability tricks: QK-norm or QK-clip).

name: Graph neural network message passing (GCN and GAT)
formula: general: h_v^(l+1) = UPDATE(h_v^(l), AGGREGATE({h_u^(l) : u a neighbor of v})) ; GCN: H^(l+1) = σ(D̃^(−1/2) × Ã × D̃^(−1/2) × H^(l) × W^(l)), Ã = A + I, D̃ = degree matrix of Ã ; GAT: α_vu = softmax over neighbors u of LeakyReLU(aᵀ × [W × h_v, W × h_u]), h_v' = σ(sum over u of α_vu × W × h_u)
meaning: Each node updates its vector from its neighbors' vectors; the GCN (Kipf and Welling) uses a degree-normalized average including the node itself, and the graph attention network (GAT) learns attention weights over neighbors. Self-attention is message passing on a fully connected graph.
used_for: GraphCast weather forecasting (Google DeepMind, 2023), GNoME materials discovery (2023), molecule and drug models, travel-time prediction in Google Maps, recommendation graphs (PinSage). Book toy: averaging own and friends' jazz scores. In the book: Chapter 17 (Graph neural networks: when data is a web, not a line).
